segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers and sisters, knowing that we will receive a stricter judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we all stumble in many ways. If anyone does not stumble in speech, that person is perfect, able to bridle the whole body as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now if we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we steer their whole body as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look at ships as well: though they are so large and are driven by harsh winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the impulse of the helmsman wishes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So too the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. See how small a fire kindles how great a forest!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the tongue is a fire. The tongue is set among our members as the world of unrighteousness; it stains the whole body, sets the wheel of existence ablaze, and is itself set ablaze by Gehenna.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For every kind of wild animal and bird, of reptile and sea creature, is being tamed and has been tamed by humankind,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but the tongue no human being can tame—a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who have been made in the likeness of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From the same mouth come blessing and curse. My brothers and sisters, these things ought not to be so.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Does a spring gush sweet and bitter water from the same opening?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Can a fig tree, my brothers and sisters, produce olives, or a grapevine figs? Nor can salt water produce sweet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who among you is wise and understanding? Let that person show, by a good way of life, works done in the gentleness of wisdom.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, do not boast and lie against the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is not the wisdom that comes down from above; it is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For where there is jealousy and selfish ambition, there is unrest and every worthless practice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peaceable, considerate, willing to yield, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, without hypocrisy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

notes.note: Some manuscripts read “Look” (the reading behind the King James “Behold”) instead of “Now if.” The two Greek expressions were pronounced alike in the period and were easily confused by copyists. The text follows the reading printed in SBLGNT and most modern editions.

The grammar and punctuation of this sentence are disputed. The phrase can be attached to what precedes (“the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness”) or, as here, taken as what the tongue represents among the parts of the body: the unrighteous world in miniature. Either way the tongue is pictured as the place where the world’s wrongdoing is concentrated in a person.

notes.traditional: the course of nature; the whole course of life
notes.note: The Greek is literally “the wheel of origin” or “of becoming.” Similar expressions were used in Greek religious and philosophical circles for the cycle of birth and death, but most scholars think that by this time the phrase had become a general expression for the whole round of human life. The image of the wheel is kept rather than paraphrased; the exact nuance is uncertain.

Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which had become the standard Jewish image for the place of final judgment. Many translations render it “hell,” usually with a footnote; the name is kept here so that it is not merged with Hades or with later imagery. This is the only occurrence of the word in the New Testament outside the Gospels.

The traditional “meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a humble, unassertive manner, here set against the jealousy and ambition of the next verse. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the usual rendering in modern translations.

This word is rare outside the New Testament. Older translations linked it with a similar-sounding word for strife, but its few earlier occurrences concern self-seeking pursuit of position, and most modern scholars and translations render it “selfish ambition” or “rivalry.” The precise sense remains somewhat uncertain.

The adjective comes from the word for “soul” or “life” and describes what belongs to ordinary human life as opposed to what comes from God’s Spirit. The older rendering “sensual” wrongly suggests bodily appetites, and “natural” can sound like praise. Paul and Jude use the word in the same contrast with “spiritual.”

The word can mean either “not making distinctions,” that is, impartial, or “not divided,” that is, unwavering. James uses the related verb in both senses, for wavering in 1:6 and for discriminating between people in 2:4. Either meaning fits here, and scholars are divided.

The Greek can equally mean “for those who make peace,” making the peacemakers the ones who benefit from the harvest rather than the ones who sow. Translations are divided between the two. “Fruit of righteousness” is likewise open to two readings: the fruit that consists in righteousness, or the fruit that righteousness produces.

Greek has a single word family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” and the verb traditionally rendered “justify.” The righteousness here belongs to the same family as the verb “justified” in 2:21–25. It means being in the right and doing what is right.

candidates.reason: The plural address to a mixed congregation recurs throughout the letters, and translations vary between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters,” and “friends,” so one policy is needed.
It recurs in Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and James, and translators divide between “perfect,” “mature,” and “complete,” which affects how readers hear the demand.
The word covers both commendable zeal and destructive jealousy or envy across many books, and the English for the negative sense should be uniform.
It appears in several vice lists in Paul as well as here, and translations vary between “selfish ambition,” “rivalry,” and “strife.”

It occurs in 1 Corinthians 2 and 15, in Jude 19 and here, always in contrast with “spiritual,” and the renderings “natural,” “unspiritual,” “worldly,” and “sensual” give readers very different impressions.
